AI agents may be able to place orders for customers, but retailers still decide whether to let them access their sites. Amazon has blocked personal agents, while Walmart has welcomed them.

DoorDash is taking a route that combines outside access with its own tools. The company wants to work with third-party agent makers and has released a tool that enables other chatbots to place corporate orders. It has also launched its own chatbot and text-to-order service.

So far, DoorDash says it has received “several hundred” orders in total from third-party agents. Most customers still place orders through its app, according to CEO Tony Xu.

messages.content:
Write a LinkedIn post based on the article below. Use your judgment about the angle, voice, length, structure and ending.

<constraints>
- Return plain prose without hashtags, emojis, decorative symbols, headings, bold text, bullet points or numbered lists.
- Avoid successive isolated one-sentence paragraphs and sequences of clipped sentences or fragments used for drama. An occasional short sentence is fine when it serves the point.
- State claims directly. Avoid rhetorical reframing such as "This isn't X; it's Y," "X, not Y," and "not X, but Y." Keep necessary factual distinctions.
- State additional capabilities directly, without "not just X," "not only X" or "more than just X" constructions.
- Omit interchangeable slogans, generic scene-setting, teaser questions and labels announcing an insight, such as "Here's the thing," "The real story," or "The takeaway?" Start with the substance.
- Replace generic benefit claims and inflated significance with the actual change or consequence. Avoid promises to "unlock potential," "transform everything" or "change the game."
- Use plain words and direct verbs. Avoid prestige vocabulary, corporate jargon and noun-heavy phrases when ordinary wording says the same thing.
- Connect ideas through their actual relationship. Avoid stock pivots such as "But here's the catch," "Let that sink in," or "And that's where things get interesting."
- Avoid invented objections, staged revelations and claims that a point is "honest," "uncomfortable" or "what nobody is talking about."
- Do not force ideas into groups of three, matching sentence templates, decorative "from X to Y" ranges or repeated short payoff lines. Let the content determine the rhythm.
- Avoid trailing significance clauses such as ", highlighting the importance of..." or ", underscoring the need for..." State a useful point directly or omit it.
- Keep uncertainty where it is needed, without stacked hedges, repeated qualifications or intensifiers added for emphasis.
- Avoid recap endings, universal lessons, generic predictions and requests for reactions such as "Thoughts?" or "Agree?" Stop when the post has said what it needs to say.
- Do not invent personal experiences, testing, conversations, emotions or discovery stories for the person publishing the post.
- Avoid repeated em dashes, ellipses, exclamation marks or rhetorical questions used to manufacture suspense or emphasis.
</constraints>

<linkedin_post>DoorDash says it has received “several hundred” orders in total from third-party AI agents. For comparison, the company reported an average of 3 million deliveries a day in 2025.

That gap suggests agent-based ordering is still small for DoorDash, though the figures cover different periods and are not directly comparable. CEO Tony Xu said customers continue to order predominantly through the DoorDash app.

DoorDash is exploring the channel while building its own ordering tools, including a chatbot that accepts prompts and photos. Xu also raised the possibility of advertising within third-party agents.

Access remains an open question for companies building those agents. Amazon has blocked personal agents, while Walmart has welcomed them. Whether an agent can place an order may depend as much on the retailer’s policies as on the technology itself.</linkedin_post>

<linkedin_post>DoorDash is preparing for customers to order through AI agents even though it has seen only “several hundred” orders in total from third-party agents so far. Most customers still use its app, CEO Tony Xu said.

The company has introduced several ways to order using AI, including a chatbot that accepts prompts and photos and a text-to-order agent. It also offers a way for other chatbots to place corporate orders.

DoorDash wants to work with third-party agent makers, and Xu suggested advertising within those agents could become an opportunity. If customers begin ordering through an agent instead of browsing an app, restaurants and delivery platforms may need new ways to make their offers visible at the point of choice.</linkedin_post>
